title: The Calendar as a Legal Strategy
hook: Courts avoid changing election rules close to voting day. That gives a litigant a strange incentive: argue the other side sued too early, and the clock does the rest.
key_points: The Purcell principle warns federal courts against last-minute changes to voting rules before an election.
The rationale is practical — late changes confuse voters and administrators who have already begun preparing.
A March 2026 executive order on mail-in voting and citizenship verification was blocked from full implementation by a federal court in Boston.
The administration, joined by twelve states led by Alabama, asked the Supreme Court's emergency docket to clear the way.
Its central argument is timing: the challengers sued too soon, before any concrete harm.
If that succeeds, revived suits land closer to November — when Purcell itself can be raised to keep courts out.
content_html: There is a sensible-sounding rule of thumb in American election law called the Purcell principle: federal courts should be reluctant to change voting rules in the run-up to an election, because late changes confuse voters and scramble the work of officials already printing ballots and training poll workers. The mail-in voting dispute now at the Supreme Court shows how a sensible rule can become a tactic.
extra_html:
In March 2026 the president signed an executive order on citizenship verification and what the order calls integrity in federal elections. A federal court in Boston blocked the government from fully implementing it, after challengers described the scheme as an unprecedented voter-verification and ballot-interception program. The administration — joined by twelve states led by Alabama — went to the Supreme Court's emergency docket asking that implementation be allowed to proceed.

As SCOTUSblog's Kelsey Dallas and Blake Fox explain, the government's central argument is not really about mail ballots at all. It is that the challengers sued too soon, before anyone had suffered concrete harm. Accept that, and the states must wait and refile — by which point the litigation sits much nearer the November election, exactly the window in which Purcell counsels judges to stay out. The result is a pincer familiar to election lawyers: a challenge can be premature one month and untimely the next, with very little space in between. Whatever one thinks of the underlying order, the episode is a good illustration that in litigation over elections, the calendar is often as decisive as the constitutional argument.

related.title: Mail Ballot Grace Periods
related.hook: A ballot mailed on Election Day can still arrive days later. Should it count? States disagree — and in 2026 the Supreme Court sided with the states that say yes.

related.title: The Supreme Court's 'Shadow Docket'
related.hook: Most Supreme Court rulings today aren't fully-argued opinions — they're fast, often unsigned orders with little explanation. In the term ending October 2025, those quietly became the majority.

related.title: Proof of Citizenship to Vote
related.hook: Should you have to show a passport or birth certificate to register to vote? A fight in Congress over that single requirement reveals a deep tension in election design.

related.title: A Law Can Take Effect Before Courts Decide If It's Legal
related.hook: Texas requires parental permission before minors can download most apps. Courts haven't ruled it constitutional — but the Supreme Court's emergency docket let it take effect anyway.

flashcards.prompt: What is the Purcell principle, and what is the reasoning behind it?
flashcards.back_html: A norm that federal courts should avoid changing voting rules shortly before an election, because late changes confuse voters and disrupt administrators who have already started preparing.

flashcards.prompt: How can a 'you sued too soon' argument end up shielding a rule from review altogether?

choices.text: Dismissing early suits pushes any refiled challenge close to the election, where Purcell counsels courts not to intervene
It converts the case into a criminal matter outside the courts' reach
It transfers jurisdiction permanently to state courts

flashcards.explanation_html: Too early and the case is premature; too late and Purcell applies. The timing arguments can squeeze the window for review from both ends.
